newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers keep up blockades after talks fail.
newsitem.headline: French truckers keep up blockades after talks fail.

text.p: Striking truck drivers kept up an 11-day stranglehold on the French economy on Thursday, ignoring government appeals to return to work after marathon talks with bosses collapsed over pay demands.
Truckers maintained almost 250 blockades on main roads and at key industrial sites. The action has brought petrol rationing in some areas, closed factories and trapped hundreds of foreign trucks.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons said the 75-hour talks led by government mediator Robert Cros had ended in "success" with a "positive result" and said truckers should lift the roadblocks strangling France.

He said agreement had been reached on truckers' demands for retirement at 55 instead of 60 and on working hours, even though there was still discord over pay. "I would not understand if the roads continued to be blocked," Pons said.

But the main unions -- the pro-Socialist CFDT, the Communist-led CGT and the non-partisan Force Ouvriere -- all told workers to stick to their roadblocks after negotiations with haulage employers broke down around midnight.
"In the present situation, especially on the issue of working hours, conditions are not right to lift the barricades," said CFDT negotiator Claude Debons.
The state traffic information centre counted 244 blockades on major highways on Thursday morning, little changed from 247 on Wednesday. Snow and sleet fell overnight in some areas.
Marc Blondel, national leader of Force Ouvriere, appealed to the centre-right government to make one more mediation attempt. "Talks must continue," he told Europe 1 radio. "The big problem is wages."
Haulage firms were offering a one percent raise and a one-time bonus of 1,500 francs ($300). Unions are demanding pay hikes that amount to an average 23 percent.

But Blondel, whose union helped spearhead a crippling 24-day round of anti-government public sector strikes in 1995, stopped short of urging an extension of the dispute to other sectors. He urged truckers to "stay calm and not respond to provocations".

Jehan de Marne, representing the employers, blamed the unions for the breakdown. "The sticking point is that our negotiating partners will not acccept or recognise the positive character of our proposals," he said.
The two sides agreed to meet on Friday to sign a deal on some issues, notably the right to retire at 55 after 25 years at the wheel, which had been resolved on Wednesday.

Snow and sleet in several areas of northern and eastern France, including some Paris suburbs, brought new misery to motorists trying to find a way around the truckers' blockades -- and Pons may be gambling it will also weaken truckers' resolve.

Barricades around petrol depots and 12 of 13 refineries across France have closed up to 2,000 of the country's 18,000 petrol stations. Petrol rationing was imposed in some areas so supplies could be maintained for fire engines and ambulances.
Police were called to several petrol stations where irate motorists refused to allow emergency vehicles, including doctors' cars, to jump queues.
The roadblocks have forced closure of some factories and cut supplies of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit.
Farmers reported shortages of animal feed as grain shipments were hit. The strike was also disrupting mail deliveries.
The strike and a parallel one in Denmark caused problems in other European countries, clogging highways and ports and disrupting commerce.
